title: Effects of resveratrol on the lipid profile of post-menopause women: Systematic review and meta-analysis - ScienceDirect
abstract:
This study aims to evaluate the effects of using resveratrol on the lipid profile of postmenopausal women. We conducted a systematic review using search terms like “postmenopausal” and “resveratrol” and their synonyms. Two reviewers handled study selection and data extraction. Randomized clinical trials assessing resveratrol in post-menopausal women were included. The meta-analysis on total cholesterol levels found no significant difference between groups, Standardized Mean Difference (SMD) −0.09 (95 % Confidence Interval (CI) −0.39 to 0.22, p = 0.59; I2 = 0 %, 2 studies, low-quality evidence).

Thus, this study systematically reviews the effects of resveratrol supplementation on the lipid profile in postmenopausal women, as well as examining urogenital symptoms, quality of life, and depressive symptoms. A systematic review was conducted following the guidelines of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) statement [12]. The study protocol was submitted to the International Prospective Registry of Ongoing Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) (number: CRD42023439223).
Key proposed mechanisms include: Activation of Sirtuin 1 (SIRT1): SIRT1 is a protein crucial for cellular aging and metabolic regulation; Antioxidant activity: Resveratrol neutralizes free radicals and protects cells from oxidative stress; Modulation of inflammation: It may reduce · The results of this review indicate that resveratrol supplementation alone did not produce significant effects on lipid profile, sleep disorders, quality of life, depressive and urogenital symptoms, or bone health.
Visceral adiposity, which is characteristic of postmenopause, contributes to an unfavorable metabolic profile, increasing cardiovascular risk. Additionally, menopause is associated with neurodegenerative changes, manifested by cognitive dysfunction and mood alterations [7,8]. Resveratrol, a polyphenol found in grape skins, red and purple fruits, peanuts, and wine, possesses beneficial properties such as reducing oxidative stress, inhibiting glycation, combating neurodegeneration, and slowing aging [9]. In humans, resveratrol is generally well-tolerated, with no adverse effects observed at oral doses in animal studies.
